clue.text: Heavenly body a body-builder possibly creates

blocks.note: taken as written
an anabolic steroid is something that builds up the body's muscle

explanation.surface: A gym fanatic is said to turn into a star, a celestial figure of a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Body-builder' reads as a muscleman, but here it is the drug that builds bodies.
explanation.definitionFit: An asteroid is a small rocky object orbiting the sun, so it counts as a celestial object.

clue.text: Jack thus appears with stringed instrument complete

blocks.note: a jack is a sailor, and AB is an able seaman
so means in this way
the lute is a plucked stringed instrument

explanation.surface: Jack turns up with his guitar and the line-up is complete.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack (as in Jack Tar) is a sailor, and AB, able-bodied seaman, is the standard crossword sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: Absolute means total or entire, as in an absolute disaster, a synonym for complete.

clue.text: Brave emblem. Sort of temple too?

indicators.note: a sort of something is a variant, so the letters are reworked into another form

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A courageous badge, with a hint that it is a kind of temple as well.
explanation.walkthrough: A brave is a Native American warrior; 'Brave' looks like an adjective meaning courageous.
explanation.definitionFit: A totem pole is a carved post bearing a tribe's crests, an emblem of the Native American peoples of the Pacific coast.

clue.text: Mountains of fruit - nothing less

indicators.note: less means without, so the named thing is taken away

blocks.note: the citrus fruit
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Huge heaps of fruit, with nothing missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mountains of fruit' suggests a glut; mountains is the definition and the fruit loses its O.
explanation.definitionFit: A range is a line of connected mountains, such as the Pennine range.

clue.text: Evidence of pressure in publishing house

blocks.note: first meaning: a mark left by pressing
second meaning: a brand name under which a publisher issues books

explanation.surface: Signs of stress at a publishing firm.
explanation.definitionFit: An imprint is a mark pressed into a surface, and also the name of a publisher's line of books.

clue.text: Ring police, say, to get Serjeant

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the words and keep the sounds rather than the spellings

blocks.note: to ring someone is to give them a buzz
fuzz is slang for the police

explanation.surface: Someone phones the police to summon a sergeant.
explanation.walkthrough: Serjeant Buzfuz is the blustering barrister for the plaintiff in Dickens's Pickwick Papers; serjeant here is the old legal rank, not the police one.
explanation.definitionFit: Buzfuz holds the rank of serjeant-at-law in Dickens's novel, so the title names that fictional character.

clue.text: Best without opponents

blocks.note: first meaning: having no equal
second meaning: not paired up against anyone

explanation.surface: Top of the field because nobody else turned up.
explanation.definitionFit: Unmatched means without equal, so the finest; literally it also means lacking a partner to play against.

clue.text: Obscure old codger accepts a thousand dollars

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a fogy is a fussy old-fashioned person
G is short for a grand, a thousand dollars

explanation.surface: An unknown elderly man takes a thousand-dollar bribe.
explanation.definitionFit: Foggy means unclear or hazy, as in a foggy memory, which is to say obscure.

clue.text: An astronomical overhead

blocks.note: surface reading: a running cost of a business that is enormous
setter's reading: the point in the sky directly above, in the astronomer's sense

explanation.walkthrough: 'Astronomical overhead' sounds like a huge business expense; read literally it is the sky point straight above an observer.
explanation.definitionFit: The zenith is the point of the celestial sphere vertically above an observer, an astronomical term.

clue.text: Judges under pressure?

blocks.note: first meaning: estimates or assesses
second meaning: instruments that sit under pressure and measure it

explanation.surface: Members of the bench are feeling the strain.
explanation.walkthrough: Judges is a verb here, not the people on the bench.
explanation.definitionFit: To gauge something is to estimate it, and gauges are dials that register the pressure applied to them.

clue.text: Protested notwithstanding the material

blocks.note: first meaning, read as 'protested not with standing': staged a sit-in
second meaning: a glossy woven fabric

explanation.surface: Someone objected in spite of the fabric on offer.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 'notwithstanding' into 'not with standing': a protest made sitting down is a sit-in, so the protesters SAT IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Satin is a smooth, lustrous woven fabric, a common dressmaking material.

clue.text: Sort of arming apt to make one grouse

indicators.note: a sort of something is a variant version, so the letters are rearranged into another form

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Getting ready to take up weapons is enough to make anyone complain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grouse' looks like a verb meaning complain, but it is the game bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The ptarmigan is a mountain bird of the grouse family that turns white in winter.

clue.text: Jack's business in Canada is making ungainly progress

blocks.note: first meaning: the trade of a lumberjack, felling and cutting timber, as Canadians call it
second meaning: moving heavily and clumsily

explanation.surface: A man called Jack runs a Canadian firm that is struggling along.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack is not a man's name but the lumberjack; in North America lumber is cut timber.
explanation.definitionFit: Lumbering is both the timber-cutting trade and the verb for walking in a heavy, awkward way.

clue.text: Journey's end for Feste's appointment?

blocks.note: surface reading: a travel booking for a character named Feste
setter's reading: Feste the clown in Twelfth Night sings that journeys end in lovers meeting, so the end of a journey is a lovers' date

explanation.surface: Someone arranges where a trip should finish for Feste's booking.
explanation.walkthrough: Feste's song in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night runs 'Journeys end in lovers meeting'; that meeting is the appointment.
explanation.definitionFit: A tryst is a secret arranged meeting between lovers, exactly the appointment the song promises.

clue.text: A little consideration

blocks.note: first meaning: as in 'a ... too long', slightly
second meaning: careful reflection on something

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one phrase, a small amount of care, but splits into two meanings of the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: Used adverbially, 'a thought' means slightly; as a noun it means reflection or attentive regard.

clue.text: Female materialized

blocks.note: first meaning: a woman's name
second meaning, read as 'material-ized': turned into a fabric

explanation.surface: A woman suddenly appeared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Materialized' means appeared, but the setter wants it taken as made into material.
explanation.definitionFit: Georgette is a girl's name and also a thin silk or crêpe dress fabric.

clue.text: Source of celestial music for the ball?

blocks.note: first meaning: the old idea that the heavenly bodies make a music as they turn
second meaning: a round solid object

explanation.surface: Someone asks who will supply heavenly music for a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ball' suggests a dance needing a band; it is just a round object. The music of the spheres is the ancient notion of harmony from the planets.
explanation.definitionFit: A sphere is a perfectly round body, the same shape as a ball.

clue.text: Like Byron's critics - not from Savile Row?

blocks.note: first meaning: Byron wrote that every trade needs an apprenticeship except criticism, for critics all come ready-formed
second meaning: bought off the peg rather than made to measure

explanation.surface: Byron's reviewers wore cheap suits rather than tailored ones.
explanation.walkthrough: Savile Row is the London street of bespoke tailors. Byron's English Bards and Scotch Reviewers says critics need no training: 'critics all are ready made'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ready-made describes clothes bought finished off the rack, and things or people that come already formed.

clue.text: Deliberate giving room to us

blocks.note: a studio is a working room, such as an artist's
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is intentionally making space for us.
explanation.walkthrough: Deliberate is an adjective here, meaning careful, not the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Studious can mean careful and intentional, as in studious avoidance, matching deliberate.

clue.text: Distant meteor storm

indicators.note: a storm throws things about wildly, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A shower of meteors is taking place far away.
explanation.definitionFit: Something remote is far off in space or time, a plain synonym for far away.

clue.text: Audio play-backs

blocks.note: surface reading: replaying a sound recording
setter's reading: sounds that come back naturally off a wall or cliff

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests tape machines; the answer is the natural repetition of sound, no equipment needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Echoes are sounds reflected back to the listener from a surface, so the sound plays back.

clue.text: Try hand-out from supply point

indicators.note: out here means out of order, so these letters are scrambled

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone tries giving out rations from a depot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hand-out' looks like a single word for a gift; the hyphen hides the split.
explanation.definitionFit: A hydrant is a street outlet from which water is drawn off the mains, so it is a water supply point.

clue.text: Horse observed with teeth on edge

definitions.note: describes the tool: one with teeth along its edge

blocks.note: a hack is a riding horse
past tense of see

explanation.surface: A horse was seen grinding its teeth nervously.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Teeth on edge' looks like the idiom for being irritated; read literally, it is a blade with teeth along its edge.
explanation.definitionFit: A hacksaw is a fine-toothed saw for metal, a tool whose cutting edge carries teeth.

clue.text: Repeatedly clean up with this weapon

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the letters are read from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: to mop is to clean, and repeatedly means doing it twice

explanation.surface: Someone keeps tidying away with a particular weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: Mop up is a cleaning phrase, but up is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The pom-pom was a quick-firing automatic gun, named for the sound of its shots.

clue.text: Bit of a blow in guide to weather - unsettled

indicators.note: a bit of the phrase means only a stretch of its running letters is kept

blocks.note: found running across the words blow, in and guide

explanation.surface: A weather forecast gives a gusty spell, with changeable conditions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unsettled' sounds like the weather; here it means a bill not yet paid.
explanation.definitionFit: A debt that is owing has not yet been paid, so the account is unsettled.

clue.text: I contended under cover provided by climbers

blocks.note: taken as written
to vie is to compete

explanation.surface: Someone recalls competing while sheltered by mountaineers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climbers' suggests mountaineers; here they are climbing plants.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivied means overgrown with ivy, a climbing plant that covers walls.

clue.text: Like the work of a poor writer, terribly needy

definitions.text: Like the work of a poor writer

indicators.note: terribly suggests something done badly, so the letters come out in a garbled order

blocks.note: a hack is a writer who churns out dull work for pay
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A struggling author's output is described as desperately in need.
explanation.walkthrough: The poor writer does double duty: it is part of the definition and also the hack who starts the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Hackneyed means trite and overused, which is what a hack's stale prose tends to be.

clue.text: Plane trip includes parts of Everest

definitions.note: a description of the country, which contains part of the mountain

indicators.note: to trip is to stumble, so the letters fall out of order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A flight over the Himalayas takes in sections of the world's highest mountain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trip' looks like a journey by plane; it is the scramble signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Nepal is the Himalayan kingdom whose northern border runs over the summit, so the peak lies partly within it.

clue.text: Futile to cut down use of the index-finger

definitions.text: to cut down use of the index-finger

blocks.note: first meaning: serving no purpose

blocks.clueFragment: to cut down use of the index-finger
blocks.note: second meaning, read as two words: to do less pointing

explanation.surface: It is useless to try to stop using your forefinger.
explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning splits the answer: the index finger is the one you point with, so using it less is to point less.
explanation.definitionFit: Something pointless has no purpose or effect, the same as futile.

clue.text: One way to play instrument

blocks.note: first meaning: the musical direction to play softly
second meaning: the keyboard instrument

explanation.surface: A tip on the right way to play some instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one phrase about technique; it is two meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: Piano is the Italian score marking for soft, and also the short name of the pianoforte.

clue.text: Thumb, perhaps, or end of digit put on insect

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter only
put on means placed after, joining one piece to the tail of the other

blocks.note: a midge is a tiny biting fly
the final letter of the word digit

explanation.surface: A thumb, or the tip of a finger, gets stuck onto a bug.
explanation.walkthrough: Thumb is Tom Thumb, the tiny man of folk tale and circus fame, not the digit; the actual digit is a decoy.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom Thumb was a famously tiny person, the old term for which is a midget.

clue.text: Residents number 500 with Sam and Tony

blocks.note: D is the Roman numeral for 500
Sam Weller and his father Tony are characters in Dickens's Pickwick Papers

explanation.surface: A count of local residents finds five hundred, plus two men named Sam and Tony.
explanation.walkthrough: Sam and Tony are both Wellers, Mr Pickwick's servant and his coachman father.
explanation.definitionFit: Dwellers are people who live in a place, so they are its residents or inhabitants.
